## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Huṁhuṅka Sutta* (Ud 1.4; PTS Ud 3) is a discourse in the *Bodhivagga* of the *Udāna*. Set on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, the narrative opens after the Buddha has spent seven continuous days seated in a single cross-legged position experiencing the bliss of liberation (*vimuttisukha*) [Masefield 1997]. Upon emerging from that meditative absorption, he is approached by a haughty brahmin characterized as of the "Huṁhuṅka" breed (*humhuṅkajātiko*), an epithet denoting one who recites or utters the sound *huṁ* [Masefield 1997]. The visitor inquires about what makes someone a genuine brahmin, prompting the Buddha to deliver an inspired utterance (*udāna*) defining the qualities of the true brahmin [Masefield 1997].
